# The Weight of Small Things

There's a coffee cup on my desk that's been here for three days. I know this because I can see the ring it's made on the wood, a faint brown circle that marks its territory like a claim. The coffee inside has long since turned into something that might be toxic. I keep meaning to move it but I haven't. There's something almost meditative about leaving it there, watching it become a part of the landscape.

This is what life has become for me lately—a collection of small, unmoved things. A book on the nightstand that I've been "reading" for six months. A gym membership I pay for monthly but visit maybe quarterly. A text from my sister that I've read but not answered. These aren't failures, exactly. Or maybe they are and I've just made peace with that.

I read somewhere that humans are supposed to be creatures of meaning-making. We're supposed to build narratives out of our days, construct stories that make sense. But some days I'm not sure what narrative I'm even in. Am I the protagonist? A supporting character in someone else's story? An extra, walking across the background while the real drama happens elsewhere?

The thing about being an adult is nobody tells you how much of it is just managing. Utilities, appointments, obligations, the small transactions that make up the bulk of existence. When we're young, we imagine adulthood as this expansive thing—freedom and possibility. What we don't imagine is the monotony of it all. The fact that you'll spend maybe two hours per day actually doing something you chose to do, while the rest gets consumed by the machinery of staying alive.

I watched a bird outside my window today. It was just sitting on the telephone wire, not doing anything in particular. Not eating, not preening, not preparing for anything. Just sitting. I envied it a little bit. The bird didn't have to justify its existence by being productive. It could just be.

Someone recently told me I should start a hobby. They meant well. They were worried about me, I think, though they phrased it as concern about my well-being. As if the solution to existential numbness is taking up pottery or rock climbing. Maybe they're right. Maybe my problem is that I need to feel like I'm building something. Except I've never been good at building. I've mostly just been good at getting by.

My apartment is clean but not organized. It's the kind of clean that suggests someone who does the minimum—wipes counters, sweeps floors—but doesn't address the deeper disorder. The drawer in my kitchen has become a archaeological site of dead batteries, mystery keys, and rubber bands that have lost their elasticity. I could organize it. I probably should. But what's the point? They're just going to get disordered again.

This is what I imagine people mean when they talk about depression, though I've never been officially diagnosed. It's not that everything is terrible all the time. It's that nothing seems to matter much, and simultaneously everything feels heavy. The heaviness of making lunch. The heaviness of choosing what to wear. The heaviness of deciding what to do with a Tuesday evening.

I had a dream last night that I was in my childhood home, but it was larger than I remembered. There were additional rooms that I'd somehow forgotten about—whole corridors I'd never explored. In the dream, I was searching for something but I couldn't remember what. I woke up with that same searching feeling still in my chest.

Sometimes I think about the life I thought I'd have versus the one I'm actually living. The gap between them feels like a failure that belongs specifically to me, though logically I know everyone has that gap. Nobody becomes exactly who they imagined at age sixteen. But knowing this doesn't make it better. It just makes it a universal failure, which is somehow worse.

The coffee cup is still there. Someone came into my space today and noticed it immediately, made a light comment about needing to clean up. I felt oddly defensive. The cup isn't hurting anyone. It's just sitting there, existing in its way. Maybe I'm keeping it as evidence of something—proof that time passes, that I was here yesterday, that continuity exists even if it doesn't feel meaningful.

I think about the things people say they want—happiness, success, love, purpose. They're holding these up like they're obvious, like of course these are the things worth pursuing. I'm not sure I want any of them anymore. Or I want them but don't believe they exist in the way people describe. Love seems like a marketing campaign for connection. Success seems like a way to keep score in a game nobody asked to play. Happiness sounds exhausting.

What I think I actually want is to stop trying so hard. To let myself be as unmoved as that coffee cup. To sit on a telephone wire and not have to justify it.

But I can't do that. There are obligations. There are people who would worry. There's the basic machinery of existence that requires a minimum amount of participation.

So instead I'll move the coffee cup tomorrow. I'll empty it down the sink and maybe even wash it. I'll respond to my sister's text. I'll do the small things that suggest I'm participating in life. And maybe that's enough. Maybe that's what adulthood actually is—not the building of something grand, but the honest acknowledgment that most of it is just showing up and moving the small things around until they've been moved enough times that it somehow counts as living.

The bird flew away eventually. It didn't accomplish anything by sitting on that wire. But it was there, and then it wasn't, and that was the whole story.
